title: Capacity concerns who may sue or be sued and how legal disabilities affect proceedings

content.overview: Capacity concerns who may sue or be sued and how legal disabilities affect proceedings. Indian State liability operates through Article 300 for private-law claims and through distinct constitutional remedies for certain fundamental-rights violations.
content.glance: Capacity concerns who may sue or be sued and how legal disabilities affect proceedings. Indian State liability operates through Article 300 for private-law claims and through distinct constitutional remedies for certain fundamental-rights violations.
content.study: Capacity concerns who may sue or be sued and how legal disabilities affect proceedings. Indian State liability operates through Article 300 for private-law claims and through distinct constitutional remedies for certain fundamental-rights violations.\n\nArticle 300 supplies the constitutional basis for suits by and against the Union and States. P&O Steam Navigation and Kasturi Lal form the historical sovereign-immunity line. Later cases such as Nilabati Behera developed public-law compensation for egregious constitutional wrongs, especially Article 21 violations.

sections.heading: Provenance, Legislative Objective & Doctrinal Foundations
sections.body: Article 300 supplies the constitutional basis for suits by and against the Union and States. P&O Steam Navigation and Kasturi Lal form the historical sovereign-immunity line. Later cases such as Nilabati Behera developed public-law compensation for egregious constitutional wrongs, especially Article 21 violations.

sections.heading: Textual Anatomy, Provisos & Statutory Deconstruction
sections.body: Article 300 addresses governmental legal personality; CPC provisions govern procedural requirements for suits against government. Constitutional compensation under Articles 32 and 226 is distinct from an ordinary private-law damages action.

sections.heading: Mandatory Proving Ingredients & Essential Elements
sections.body: 1. Identify claimant and defendant capacity. 2. Classify the action as private-law or constitutional. 3. Identify the source of duty. 4. Check CPC procedural preconditions. 5. Establish breach, causation and recoverable loss.

sections.heading: Evidentiary Burdens under BSA 2023 (ss. 104–106 & s. 63)
sections.body: The claimant must prove the factual wrong and causation. Official records, custody documents, medical evidence and witness testimony may be central. Constitutional compensation is a public-law remedy and does not simply restate an ordinary tort action.

sections.heading: Procedural Roadmap, Competent Forum & Limitation Act Checkpoints
sections.body: Private-law suits against government are governed by CPC provisions including Sections 79 and 80 where applicable. Constitutional compensation may be sought under Articles 32 or 226 where the facts disclose a public-law violation. Limitation must be checked separately for civil claims.

examples.title: Illustration 1 — Doctrine Satisfied
examples.body: Sovereign-immunity principles in private law must be distinguished from constitutional compensation for established fundamental-rights violations. The claimant must still prove the remaining ingredients on the civil standard.

examples.title: Illustration 2 — Boundary Defect
examples.body: Article 300 establishes governmental legal personality; the scope of immunity is governed by precedent and constitutional remedies. A court should not infer liability from the label alone.

distinctions.title: Private tort suit vs Constitutional compensation
distinctions.right: A tort suit is an ordinary civil action; constitutional compensation is a public-law remedy for an established constitutional wrong.

rows.left: Sovereign-immunity principles in private law must be distinguished from constitutional compensation for established fundamental-rights violations.
rows.right: A tort suit is an ordinary civil action; constitutional compensation is a public-law remedy for an established constitutional wrong.

rows.left: Apply the ingredients of the pleaded tort.
rows.right: Do not substitute the neighbouring cause of action.
